title: Youth Engagement
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about young people as agents of change -- the movements they have led, the debate over the voting age, and how they shape society even without the vote.
competenceGoals: reflect on how young people can participate and influence society at local, national, and global levels
explore and discuss what it means to be an active citizen in a democratic society

content.content:
## Apathetic? Think again

Young people are sometimes dismissed as politically apathetic -- too busy with social media and entertainment to care about the world around them. But history tells a very different story. From the student movements of the 1960s to the climate strikes of the 2010s and 2020s, young people have repeatedly stood at the forefront of social and political change. Far from being bystanders, they have often been the ones pushing societies forward.

This chapter takes that history seriously. We will look at how young people have shaped politics and society over time, the current forms of youth engagement in English-speaking countries, the debate about lowering the voting age, and the real challenges facing young people who want to make a difference. The central theme is that age and the formal right to vote are not the only measures of political power -- young people have repeatedly proven they can be powerful agents of change even without them.

## Youth movements that changed history

**Youth activism** refers to political or social action carried out by young people with the goal of bringing about change -- protests, campaigning, volunteering, creating content, organising events. It often focuses on issues that disproportionately affect younger generations, such as climate change, education policy, gun violence and digital rights, and while the methods may differ from traditional politics, it has been a driving force for change throughout history. The examples are striking. The **Greensboro Sit-ins** of 1960 began when four Black students in North Carolina sat down at a whites-only lunch counter and refused to leave when denied service, sparking a wave of sit-ins across the South and a defining moment in the Civil Rights Movement. The **Soweto Uprising** of 1976 in South Africa began when students protested being forced to learn in Afrikaans; police opened fire, and the event galvanised international opposition to apartheid. **March for Our Lives** in 2018, organised by students who survived the Parkland school shooting in Florida, became one of the largest youth-led protests in American history and registered hundreds of thousands of new young voters. And **Fridays for Future**, started by Swedish teenager Greta Thunberg, spread worldwide into mass school strikes for climate action.

These movements show that young people can be powerful agents of change even when they lack formal political power such as the vote. Understanding how young people develop their political views helps explain why some become active and others do not. The key concept here is **political socialisation** -- the lifelong process through which individuals develop their political attitudes, values and behaviours. It begins in childhood and continues throughout life, shaped by family, school, peer groups, media and personal experiences. For young people, school and social media are particularly important in shaping their understanding of politics and their willingness to participate. This is why civic education and the information environment matter so much: they are part of how the next generation of citizens is formed.

content.content:
## The voting age debate, and participation today

One of the most discussed questions about youth participation is whether the voting age should be lowered from 18 to 16 -- and it is worth presenting both sides fairly. The arguments *for* lowering it are substantial: 16-year-olds can work, pay taxes and drive in many countries, so arguably should have a say in how their taxes are spent; early voting habits tend to stick, so voting at 16 may build lifelong participation; Scotland let 16-year-olds vote in the 2014 independence referendum, where turnout among 16-17 year-olds reached 75 percent; young people are affected by decisions on education, climate and housing; and it could encourage schools to strengthen civic education. The arguments *against* are equally serious: the brain is still developing at 16, particularly the parts responsible for long-term decision-making; 16-year-olds may be more easily influenced by parents, teachers or social media; many have limited life experience; if 16, why not 14 or 12, since the line must be drawn somewhere; and low turnout among 18-24 year-olds suggests younger voters may not use the right anyway. Currently most countries set the voting age at 18, though Scotland and Wales allow 16-year-olds to vote in some elections and Austria allows it in all elections.

Young people today participate in ways that differ from previous generations but are not necessarily less engaged. *Traditional participation* includes joining political parties (though membership is declining among the young), voting, writing to representatives and joining student councils and youth parliaments. *New forms* include social-media activism, creating and sharing content about political issues, online fundraising, digital petitions and consumer activism -- boycotting or supporting brands based on values. There are real *barriers*, honestly named: a feeling that politicians do not listen to or represent young people, a lack of civic education, the complexity of political systems, disillusionment with traditional politics, and economic pressures like housing costs and student debt. But there are also real *opportunities*: technology makes organising easier than ever, global connectivity lets young people learn from movements worldwide, and there is growing recognition that young voices matter. A useful concept tying this together is **intergenerational justice** -- the fairness of today's decisions to future generations, which gives young people a particular stake in long-term issues like climate.

content.content:
## In short

Far from being apathetic, young people have repeatedly led social and political change, from the Greensboro Sit-ins and the Soweto Uprising to March for Our Lives and Fridays for Future, proving they can be powerful agents of change even without the vote. Political socialisation -- shaped by family, school, peers and media -- explains how young people develop their political attitudes. The debate over lowering the voting age to 16 has serious arguments on both sides, from taxation and habit-forming to brain development and experience. Young people today participate through both traditional channels and new digital and consumer forms, facing real barriers like disillusionment and economic pressure but also real opportunities through technology and global connection. Intergenerational justice gives them a particular stake in the long-term decisions shaping their future.
